name: Colostrinin (PRPs)

lead: Colostrinin is a mixture of proline-rich peptides originally isolated from ewe colostrum, the first milk. Researchers describe effects on T-cell maturation and cytokine production, and it was developed for Alzheimer's disease.

In supplement and bodybuilding circles it is grouped with colostrum products used for immune support and recovery. The appearance chain is indirect: fewer illnesses, steadier training and recovery. Human trials were done in Alzheimer's patients, not on appearance outcomes.

paras: It is taken orally as a supplement, often alongside other colostrum or immune products. Users describe it as part of a recovery or immunity stack.

Safety data come from a limited set of trials in older Alzheimer's patients, mostly from one research group, and no appearance-focused safety studies exist. As an animal-derived product it is not suitable for people avoiding dairy-sourced ingredients.

angle.text: Users take it hoping to stay healthy and recover so training is not interrupted. The appearance link is indirect and not itself studied.

lead: Colostrinin (CLN), also called proline-rich polypeptides (PRP), is a complex of peptides of about 500 to 3000 Da first found as a fraction accompanying sheep colostral immunoglobulins [1][2]. It is about 25 percent proline [2].

In supplement culture it is promoted for immunity and recovery, which users link to missing fewer workouts and keeping a steady physique. Forum posts on T Nation mention proline-rich polypeptides among antiviral and immune-supportive colostrum components [3].
Research shows immunoregulatory effects in cell and animal work and clinical trials in Alzheimer's disease, where reports describe stabilised cognition [1][4][5][6].

paras: PRP is not species specific and regulates cytokines including interferon, TNF-alpha, IL-6 and IL-10 and reduces reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide production [2]. Laboratory studies report effects on T-cell maturation and on glutathione metabolism and mitochondrial function [1][5]. In vitro, it reduced amyloid-beta aggregation [7][8].

ReGen Therapeutics developed Colostrinin for Alzheimer's disease, with phase II trials under way in 2005 [9]. A 1999 double-blind placebo-controlled study and later multicentre trials in Poland were reported [10][11][12].
A 1999 study reported that colostrinin facilitated learning and memory in rats [13]. Oral dosing extended lifespan in mice in one review [5].

A 15-week double-blind phase followed by open-label treatment in 105 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease at six Polish centres examined Colostrinin against placebo [11]. A 1999 randomised double-blind study, a long-term study in 2002 and a 2009 report described benefit in stabilising cognition and daily activities [10][12][14]. A 2023 randomised placebo-controlled study of proline-rich polypeptides in adults reported changes in blood BDNF concentration alongside cognitive function [15]. No trial has measured appearance outcomes.
A 2007 review asked whether proline-rich polypeptides were a therapeutic potential or a mirage in Alzheimer's disease [16].
